utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Office of the Prosecutor, Gerard Dobbyn with Tom Hannis and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic. I would like to apologise. It was misunderstanding, that we are starting at 11.00, yesterday. So completely my fault. I, again, ask for apologies for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Dobbyn completes his examination-in-chief, I remind the witness that he is still on his oath. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's what comes when relying on one's memory rather than looking at the notes. My apologise, Mr. Zecevic. Please resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could the witness please be shown 1D03-4106.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is your statement from 1995, sir. We received it yesterday. Let me go back to one question we discussed yesterday. Your detention, namely; you call it arrest. Early on 3rd or 4th March 1992. You told the Prosecutor or myself that completely blameless you were taken to the police station and beaten up by this man Hrsum; and when you were asked by the Prosecutor what kind of injuries you sustained, you said this man Hrsum punched you in the face and beat you with a club or truncheon on the back. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then the Prosecutor asked you if Malko Koroman had noticed the injuries to your face and if he had taken any steps about that, and you said, to the best of your knowledge, he didn't do anything?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement -- may page 2 be shown to you, please. In 1995, you stated that this man, Hrsum, who had interrogated you, slapped you a couple of times - that means with an open hand, not a fist - and hit you with a truncheon on the back. The discrepancy is small, but it is important to know whether slaps in the face leave visible traces. They don't. But if he punched you in the face, you would have visible injuries. It's important to know, therefore, which of the two it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I'd just like to intervene at this point. I understand that we rely on translations here, but the -- what's being put to the witness, according to the English translation at least, is incorrect. The English translation we have reads that he was punched in the face. There's no mention of slapping. And it doesn't say anything being slapped or punched just a couple of times. But that's what has been put to the witness at the moment. He has been told that the statement contains those words. So I wonder if we can clarify this. At some point, perhaps if the B/C/S is read and then that's translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 3 of your statement. It begins with the word "Immediately," "Odmah."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, can you direct me to where on page 3 that is? I'm looking at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It states on page 2: "I explained to him who had sent me -- or, rather, no one had sent me, and he started punching me in the face right away."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I'm sorry. It's page 2 of the Serbian transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, sir, on page 2, halfway down the page, it begins with the word "Odmah." There is a reference to the 3rd or 4th of March, and then it says: "He started immediately to question me as to who had sent me to guard duty."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said he started asking me, Who sent you and where are you going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that question, sir. In this statement you said, at least that's how it was recorded in the statement before the investigating judge, that Hrsum immediately started beating you with his hands on the face.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comes after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With a hand means an open hand.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also with a hand. You can have it in a clenched fist or an open hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean it was a punch?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you complain to anyone about this mistreatment that you had undergone on the 3rd or 4th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I complained to my nearest and dearest and my neighbours. I did not dare complain to the authorities, lest I be subjected to even worse things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to your statement, you were mistreated by a member of the MUP, the police. Why did you not approach the Ministry of the Interior to ask for an explanation or indemnity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the policemen belonging to the Ministry of the Interior arrested me in the way I described in my statement, whom was I supposed to approach to ask for further protection? We did ask for protection, and then we received a final answer, as I said yesterday. They did not want to live with us Muslims in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm begging you, please, to concentrate and answer my question. Pale is 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20-something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior is in Sarajevo. Why did you not approach the Ministry of the Interior to register that incident, if nobody else did that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were police administrations in Pale and in Sarajevo. Whatever I'm supposed to complain about, I was supposed to do it in my own police station in my place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But if the policemen from that police station in your place of residence mistreated you, you should have gone to the Ministry of the Interior, and the minister was Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are now going into politics, and these politics had led to the war in the first place, and what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the minister of the interior of the Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, on 3rd and 4th of March, 1992, was Mr. Alija Delimustafic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you still did not report the incident?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is it your position that the witness was not subjected to mistreat upon his arrest?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not my position. I'm just -- the point of the question was Mr. Dobbyn's question and confirmation by this witness that Mr. Malko Koroman didn't act upon it, upon allegedly seeing his bruises or knowing that he has been maltreated. And that is why I'm exploring with the witness whether he took the -- took any -- any steps to report that to the Ministry of Interior in March 1992, and he said he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what would the purpose be of exploring whether the witness, the victim himself, took any steps to report the mistreatment to the minister?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, he -- if -- if the immediate superior in the police station didn't took [sic] appropriate steps, he had the opportunity to go up and report to the ministry, and the ministry should -- would, I assume, take any -- some measures against the -- against the -- the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly. But the fact remains that he was mistreated, and so what more is there to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honours, if he didn't, then presumably he believed that -- that he has done something wrong and maybe he wasn't mistreated in a way he is representing it. Because if he was, he would have probably taken this matter to the -- to the ministry. That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And hence my original question: Whether you're disputing the fact that the witness was in fact mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't dispute that he was mistreated. I don't have the reason to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your evidence yesterday you claimed that you had been informed that late Hrvo Fehim had committed suicide, but you did not believe it because there were no traces of that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then you said the police provided security at the funeral so you couldn't see the body.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them then, but I think there were nine or ten armed policemen escorting the funeral ceremony. And when we approached to take the coffin down, they trained weapons at us. We did not stop. We took up the coffin. We didn't even expect them to shoot. But why they took down their weapons and trained them at us, I don't know. Anyway, we took the coffin towards the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you said yesterday the body was not revealed.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant it was not unbuttoned. The clothes were not unbuttoned, so we couldn't see the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you didn't do that, then how could you see if there were any traces?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see the neck, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How do you know, then - and that's what you said to the Prosecutor on page 2121 of yesterday's transcript -- sorry, page 21.1 - you said there was no investigation into the death of Hrvo Fehim. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no investigation into his death, into the death of Nasko Smaic, Izet Jasarevic, Alija Jusufovic. In none of these cases had there been an investigation into their killing, and they were all killed in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which prison do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one in the cinema hall next to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know there had been no investigation? If they were killed in the prison and you were not in the prison, how do you know that there had been no inquiry?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have happened without us hearing about it. The investigators would have come to the house of the dead people or the neighbouring houses. That would have been logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, that's a logic I don't understand. You were talking about that cinema hall. Was there any other prison in the territory of Pale that you know of?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you. As far as I know, every police station in the world must have premises for detention on the same premises. In the same way, the station of Pale had one. I had never been to such a room myself because I was held in the office and in the hallway next to it. Those people had been detained in the cinema hall. I know that the cinema hall was a place where they took people who had been arrested and people were held there. I don't know of any other prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But in the same way you know about the cinema hall, would you have known about other prisons that existed while you were in Pale.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement the witness gave in 1995. He discussed it yesterday and today, and he stands by that statement. So if there is no objection, I would like to tender it before I show him the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you have the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D03 -- just a moment. 1D03-4106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, am I to understand from your last line of questions that you're challenging adjudicated facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1311 and 1314. I'm persuing that line now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I want to show the witness another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm about to show you the aerial photograph again, the photograph of the centre of Pale, and I will ask you to comment when I ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, can you -- you remember that yesterday you marked the SJB yesterday and the cinema hall, and the place from which -- or, rather, where allegedly Karadzic gave his speech and the buses. You marked that on the photograph yesterday; remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember where the sports centre of Pale is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can see the sports ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But was there a gymnasium of sorts?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as part of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see it in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elementary school? I can't see the elementary school in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- and the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What's -- what is this cultural centre? Can you please mark its location. You will be given a pen by the usher. But I see that you know what to do anyway.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please place a number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is the cultural centre. And that is the place where you said yesterday Karadzic gave his speech when you heard him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, in this photograph, sir, we cannot see the gymnasium that belonged to the school. I believe it is to the right.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what was there in this cultural centre in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1992, the Srna TV moved in there, but also the Government of the RS. How long they stayed there, I don't know. When I left, they were still there. Later, they built government facilities at Korane, and they built one-storey buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in this culture centre which you marked with the number 1 where you say Karadzic gave his speech, that was the headquarters of the Srna News Agency of the RS and the seat of government while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were antennas, and I thought it could be TV. But those may have been antennas for government communications or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But certainly you are sure that there was no prison in that culture centre.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the same goes for the gymnasium, I suppose. You would have known if there had been a prison there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that not far from the school, behind it, there was a gymnasium for the elementary school pupils, but I don't know of a prison there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we mark this document to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D330, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand your concerns, but there are different markings on the previous document because there's four other issues -- or -- or buildings marked on that -- on that particular document. And this document we will use to challenge the Adjudicated Fact 1314. That is the purpose of -- of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the same building is marked on two different pictures. It would seem to me that one photo would be enough, showing where the building is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I certainly cannot disagree with Your Honours on that. It's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let me ask you one thing. Do you know where Donja Vinca in the Pale municipality is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the village. How far is it from Pale, from the place where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the village was shelled somewhere in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I didn't know that. But do you know what kind of village it is, who lives there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you have no information about it. Tell me, yesterday in your evidence you mentioned trucks with people from Bratunac that you saw, and you marked them on -- in that photograph, and you spoke to the drivers?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't speak to any one of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you know that the trucks with those unfortunate people were brought to Pale. You know that. And you were present?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, and I heard -- or I witnessed that by chance, and I later on told myself, Why on earth was I there at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that those people spent barely two days in Pale and they moved on to the territory controlled by the Muslims. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know what happened with these people later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. Tell me, yesterday during the examination-in-chief, there was a question about the Crisis Staff and the participation of Muslims in the activities of the Crisis Staff of Pale. And you said, I believe, that you knew nothing about that; namely, of the presence of any one Muslim in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And it wasn't possible for any Muslims be to a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Asim Zec?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Asim Zec was president of the Crisis Staff of Vrace?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never a Crisis Staff in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the late Alija Prazina, from Hrenovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the name, but I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of him being the president of the Crisis Staff of Hrenovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know who Ahmet Palo is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ahmet Palo was president of the SDA of Pale and the vice-president of the municipality, correct, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, early on. When the parties sort of established municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, in 1992, he was vice-president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he was really a puppet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But he was president of the SDA committee in Pale.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was close to that party. But let me tell you, I wasn't a member of the SDA. I wasn't really familiar with the positions, but -- but I saw that they were all carried off by the current.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the campaign of collecting weapons in Hrenovica. That was in mid-May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the day, but it was in May. I believe it was in the first half. I may have made a mistake mentioning the date because I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's a fact that the patrol in which there were two police officers -- or, rather, where two police officers were killed and five injured, that this incident happened immediately before that campaign or during that operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police officers came to harm during that operation, but, sir, that wasn't a patrol that collected weapons. That was a military operation. You may have the documents about it. And the documents read: military operation. Military operations are not conducted for collecting weapons. Everybody knows what military operations are for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after that operation, you said that Mr. Malko Koroman with tears in his eyes appeared on TV and said that the war had come to Pale, and he appealed to non-Serbs to return their weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about these persons we mentioned a short while ago: Nasko Smaic, then Jasarevic, of who you said that they were killed in prison. Do you know if they were arrested during that operation or on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't live in Hrenovica. They lived in the urban part of Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know, sir, that they were killed in prison? Where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the funerals. Didn't I say yesterday that volunteers were sought to carry out the body of Fehim Hrvo from the cinema hall. I said that when I sat on the bus I saw that there was -- they were digging a pit in the graveyard. And then there was Nezir and Alija Jusufovic and Nasko Smaic. Only Nasko Smaic was buried at Majdani, not in the centre part of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, these are criminal proceedings, so we must be very clear. If I understood you correctly, you were present at the funeral of Fehim Hrvo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for this man Jasarevic, you saw that from the bus.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That he was being buried?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Nasko Smaic, you only heard of him. You weren't present and didn't see?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, I looked from my house. The body was being transported, and five or six people were going toward the cemetery. And I couldn't go because I didn't dare move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But how did you get the information that they were killed in prison?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nasko Smaic was first taken to prison and then released. On the same day, they took him back to prison, though, and he didn't come out of it alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that's what you heard?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard as much. But it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also heard about this Jasarevic. You weren't in prison?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, but I saw the man being buried. And he was -- he had been taken to prison because he had destroyed his shop. He didn't want to give it up to anyone else, and that's why he was taken to prison and killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And his shop was at Korane.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you say that you couldn't leave your house and you saw that -- these five or six people on -- in the funeral party. How could they leave their house?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't dare leave my house and move -- I didn't say I couldn't move about Pale. I saw those people from Bratunac. How could I have seen them otherwise? I didn't lock myself up in the house. You can't put that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you moved about Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, since I saw these things. But I couldn't leave my -- the boundaries of my own local commune. I couldn't go to another local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your local commune?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you were not able to go to other local communes, then how did you come to testify that in the local commune of Korane the sale of goods to Muslim was forbidden?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people next door had a flat in Korane. He built a house next to mine. And when his children found it too hard to live up there, they moved in with the father. They said that they read those signs on shops and ran away to their father's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see that; you just heard of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people saw it with my -- with their own eyes. It's as good as myself seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you can remember, when did Nikola Koljevic come to that meeting with the representatives of the Muslim community and allegedly said that the Serbs did not wish to live with you Muslims? When was that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, even if I noted down the dates and kept a diary, it's still not certain that I would have remembered the correct date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I would remind you that you have exhausted the hour that you had requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I made the -- obviously not a very good estimation, and I'm having problems with the witness explaining the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How much time -- how much more time do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume one hour more I would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but ... I will try my best to shorten it as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly, please. If you can't remember, you can't remember. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the month of June, but which date I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On June 4, after this operation in Hrenovica when some policemen were killed, others were wounded in mid-May, on the 4th of June, 1992, more than 60 Serb soldiers were killed in an ambush at Zlovrh on the road to Zepa; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You go on about dates, and I told you a moment ago that I had never thought I would have to talk about these things before such an august international Court. Zlovrh I know, is a place name; but that battle was not at Zlovrh, and it was not for the capture of Zlovrh. I just happened to see, when I was going to attend a funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate your effort to explain, but I'm just asking you if you know that sometime in the beginning of June about 60 Serb soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. I know a lot of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that most of these people were from Pale; they were citizens of Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you testified that Karadzic had come to attend that funeral.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was talking about was not a funeral. It was some sort of rally or a meeting or whatever you want to call it. Funerals take place at cemeteries. I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was a memorial service of some sort?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you told us Karadzic came to that funeral, and he first called for tensions to be diffused, and those tensions ran high, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Karadzic was not calling for things to calm down. He was trying to ease the pain of the families. And I have to add: There was one woman who, in all likelihood, calmed those people down who lost their family members and -- by saying, These Muslims here are absolutely not to blame that my son got killed. Why were they going to Zepa? What for? I don't know that woman. I know her son was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the tension was very high; the situation was very tense?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was catastrophic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that on that occasion, in that catastrophic situation, as you call it, that was very tense, Karadzic said that by attacks Muslim houses, you protect Serb ones?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it sound illogical to you that after such a statement made by Radovan Karadzic, nobody set out to attack Muslim houses that very moment at Pale? In such a situation that was, as you said, catastrophic, the tensions ran high, many people had lost their children, 40 of them, and then he comes out with a statement like that. Wouldn't the crowd run wild and set out to destroy Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you, and you will understand doing your job you must have insight into other municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I have to tell you this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please, leave alone other municipalities. We are talking about Pale. You said you heard Karadzic say these things. It's a fact that not a single Muslim house was attacked on that day. I'm asking you: Is it logical that this didn't happen, after these words by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said. Karadzic did say that. Now, why weren't we attacked? I really cannot tell you why. I don't have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you gave before the investigating judge in Sarajevo in 1995, you made no mention of the fact that Karadzic had visited and made such a speech. And, still, it must have been etched in your memory, since you remember it to date. And you didn't mention it in your evidence in the Krajisnik case either. It's for the first time this year, in April, at the trial of Radovan Karadzic that you told this story, that Karadzic had come to the funeral and stated what he stated.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying I'm not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's not up to me to evaluate your evidence. I'm just asking you for an explanation. How is it possible that you did not mention it in 1995 or in 2004 or at the Krajisnik trial, but you mention it for the first time almost 20 years later, this April, testifying in the Karadzic trial?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the first time. Karadzic uttered these same words in other places as well. If you have an opportunity to look at video footage, you will hear Karadzic saying these very same words in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that Karadzic said the same thing in other municipalities? And then you inferred that he must have said it at Pale as well.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm trying to say. I'm telling you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you still haven't answered how it is possible that you mention this only 20 years later for the first time. And it's rather important, isn't it? That's what you haven't answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to intervene at this point because it's being put to the witness that he's never mentioned this before. And, in fact, it is referred to in his testimony in Krajisnik. I point to transcript page 5342 where he talks about Mr. Karadzic giving a speech to the population outside the TV building in Pale. It's true that he doesn't give the content of that speech in that part of the transcript. He wasn't asked about the content of the speech, but he certainly refers to Mr. Karadzic being there and giving a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's the contents we are talking about. It's not -- that's the whole issue. What Karadzic says is the -- is the issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that may be the issue, but that's what should be put to the witness, about the content. What's being put to him is that he's never mentioned any such speech at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in 1995 you did not mention it at all, that Karadzic had been to Pale; and in Krajisnik you mentioned that he had visited, you didn't say what he said; and only in April 2010, you testified in Karadzic, and here, yesterday, saying that he made that statement. I'm asking you to explain how it is possible that 18 years later you mention this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not need to talk about that when I testified against Krajisnik, because Krajisnik and Karadzic are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose, although we started a half-hour late, it would be -- it would be easier to stick to the set times, because I'm pretty sure that the accused would have been waiting in court during the break in any event. So we'll take the adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is a fact, isn't it, that after these 40 soldiers were killed at Zepa, shortly after that, 14 Serb soldiers were killed at Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, you spoke about the Red Berets from Knin. The rumour was they were in Pale, but you've never seen them; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the Red Berets for the first time from the chief of police, Malko Koroman. Before that, I didn't even know they were in Pale. But I saw them on the 2nd of July, when I set out in the convoy, near the Panorama Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You testified here that Malko Koroman informed you they were there, in Pale, and that, allegedly, he was not able to guarantee that you would be safe from them. And he didn't say what they had come to do, but, based on what you had seen on TV, you knew that they had burned down houses and killed people in Gospic, and you inferred what they were capable of doing.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Malko Koroman said the Red Berets had come from Knin to do a job. He didn't specify what job. But what else could they do other than what they had done in Knin? They had come to Pale from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the point is that you saw on TV the crimes they had committed in Gospic and Knin.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you mixed things up. Knin and Gospic are almost ethnically pure settlements in Croatia, at least they were; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were ethnically pure, these two towns, then why were those dead bodies strewn in the streets, and why were all those buildings burned?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to tell you. There was no killing or burning in Knin or Gospic because they were -- they were almost 100 per cent Serb towns, and these things are you talking about you must be confusing either with a different period or different towns.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are mixed up, not I. I know what I saw on television. I know what the anchor-man on television was showing, was saying, while the footage of these two towns was shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that the situation in Pale, because of the refugees, the war all around, and the killing of these soldiers and policemen, was extremely tense?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the Muslims, it was intolerable psychologically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is why you, representatives of the Muslim community, sought meetings and guarantees of your safety?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't ask for that just after the killing of those people. We had begged the chief of police and the president of the municipality many times before to find a way to go on living together in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown P1453.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor showed you this document. It's a letter sent by the group of citizens of the local communes of Pale and Korane, dated 9 April 1992. It is their proposal, the proposal of these citizens of Muslim ethnicity, to deal with the newly created situation concerning the arrests of unarmed members of the Muslim community. And then there's a list of proposals. Do you remember commenting this document yesterday with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see item 10 which reads -- and it's a proposal that the Muslim submit to the Crisis Staff. That persons and families who do not feel safe in the territory of Pale municipality be allowed to leave the area without hindrance and in an organised manner. In parentheses there are the reasons for that proposal. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is, as soon as 9 April, there was a proposal to make it possible for the Muslims to leave Pale without hindrance and safely, and organised -- in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're reading these documents, and you have your own position with regard to them. But when the first convoy left, I was a member of that delegation when we asked the president of the municipality, Starcevic, why those people had left, and he said they had broken the law. But what had they done? What kind of offence have they committed for you to transport them away? And he answered, It will -- it will be -- it will be known. And I said, But the same will be said of us once we leave, that we have broken the law. And that was his comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of that first convoy, which time-period are you relating to? Wasn't that late June?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are really annoying me with these dates. In a situation like that, you are doing whatever you can to save your families and your nearest and dearest. And you are now -- you now want me to give you an exact date. I really can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me when I say that certainly that first convoy did not leave before the 9th of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P1454.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document, too, was shown to you by the Prosecutor yesterday. I believe you said you had never seen this one. This is the reply of the Crisis Staff to this previous document dated 9 April, and it is dated 11 April, 1992. It is addressed to the group of Muslim citizens. And under 1 we can see there is no reason for the Muslim population to panic and move out, and it also says that the Serbian municipality of Pale shall offer full protection to all citizens, whatever their ethnicity or religion. So this was in April. And it's a reply to the previous document. As far as I remember, you are not familiar with this document. You have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this one that we see?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, can we show the witness 65 ter 2460.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a document of the Crisis Staff, that is, the Pale municipality. It's signed by Radislav Starcevic. You said that Starcevic was president of the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now we see his first name, Radislav. Does this help you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably that's what was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document deals with the change of residence of Muslim and Croatian citizens. Article 1 reads: "Citizens of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity who wish to change their residence can exercise that right with the agreement of and permission from ..." et cetera. It's a fact that under the laws of the former Yugoslavia if you change your place of residence you were obliged to go to the SJB of the place you're leaving and let them know that you're leaving and upon arriving to your new place of residence you had to register with the SJB there. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you change your residence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we who were transported to Sarajevo never went to the Pale Police Administration to let them know we're leaving. We were only put on buses, and we didn't know what would happen until we reached our destination. Nobody, in fact, went to the SJB to let them know we're leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see that it says in Article 2 that: "The change of residence will be done in an organised manner. Citizens will come to the public security station and personally apply ..."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No citizen applied for change of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's what you know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I know. I didn't do it, and nobody else do it from Pale -- did it from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, isn't the logic of an inter-ethnic conflict that members of a certain ethnic group stick together. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't agree with conflicts. If we Muslims has wanted conflict, we wouldn't have sought co-existence, and we wouldn't have asked the president of the municipality and the chief of the police to bring us someone from the top ranks of government to make a co-existence possible. And as far as conflict is concerned, at least in my municipality, there was no one Muslim who was in favour of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But your municipality is near Sarajevo, which is much bigger, with a much greater population. And you will agree with me that it is possible that the situation in Sarajevo also reflected on Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Pale used to be a suburban municipality of Sarajevo; and these reflections you're mentioning, even know, we can see where the front line of the Serbs around Sarajevo was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know. But you will agree with me when I say that many Serbs left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that they left voluntarily? I mean, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 90 per cent of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since Pale is a suburban municipality, no doubt real estate in Sarajevo is more valuable than in Pale.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there was real estate, valuable real estate in Pale too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, generally speaking, in a city it's always more expensive than in the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably don't know Sarajevo. In Sarajevo, too, there are decrepit buildings, but there are also new buildings. So you can't compare these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You exchanged your house in Pale, that is, the house of -- belonging to you and your brother, with a woman who traded in her house at Pofalici, which is in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that some people swapped houses but others didn't. They were unable to find persons to swap houses with; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that I commented that much on this yesterday. I only said that whoever didn't swap their house, the position of the police was that they had to bring the keys to the police station. Whether or not anybody did that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, how did you meet that woman?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: She came to my door-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when she did, she asked you, Do you want to swap houses with me? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: She asked my brother. I had my opinion, but my late brother was elder, so I didn't want to come forward. So, actually, my brother did it all. But I didn't oppose it because he was my elder brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your late brother basically ran this whole business about this exchange?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when you were leaving in July -- I believe you said on 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You gave that woman your keys, and I suppose that she gave you the keys to their -- to her house in Pofalici; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We saw yesterday - I don't have to show you - the contract that you signed then and had it certified by the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to comment again what I was saying yesterday. What kind of exchange is that? If I must swap one property for another and without having seen the other, and what -- what I found there is a house that was half-destroyed by an artillery shell. And, now, you tell me whether that was voluntary or involuntary. And I never moved into that house because it was -- it was demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, it's a fact that - and you confirmed a minute ago that your late brother spoke with her - the house at Pofalici, if it had not been destroyed by an artillery shell, you would have moved into that house at Pofalici temporarily?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have had to. What else could I have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the contract, which you signed with your own hand and your late brother too, and the other party, this Dragica Subotic from Pofalici, says that the parties to the agreement engaged to guard and keep the house for temporary -- for a period of time until the cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: Yes, I did sign that contract, and so did my late brother and Dragica Subotic. But in that situation, in the war, I didn't believe that I would ever be in the position to claim my house back. I'm now describing to you the situation as it was then. And I didn't really read all the provisions of the contract. This is my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But it's a fact that, eventually, that that's what really happened. You got your property back. And I suppose that Dragisa got back her destroyed house at Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank God everybody got back their property. And the state it was after the war, let me not comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, when you were leaving your house on the 2nd of July, Dragisa was present, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did Dragisa prevent you from taking out anything from your house?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't. But what could I have taken but what I was able to carry with my two hands? And where should I put it? I only grabbed the most important things, a little clothing, and off you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, sir, isn't it, that you left on a convoy, on buses, in an organised manner, precisely for reasons of safety so as not to travel in private automobiles because it was war; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably they were taking care of our safety, and we were escorted by the police all the way, at least the convoy on which I left. I cannot speak about the others, but I suppose that the others were also escorted by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "escorted by the police," that means a police vehicle went ahead of and behind the convoy accompanying the convoy; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the police saw you off to the check-point held by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How was it, then?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to the end of their combat lines, and then we had to cross the no man's land on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have the answer you gave on page 33, line 22. I said: When you say the police escorted the convoy, that means that the police vehicle went ahead of the convoy and another police vehicle was behind the convoy? And I think you answered in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that the police provided security to the convoy, for safety reasons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what reason the police escorted us, I cannot say, but they did escort us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, are you aware that some Muslims left Pale out of fear over how Sarajevo would view their staying and continuing to work in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about a doctor, Senad, from the medical centre at Pale? I don't know his last name.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. Senad, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Muslims, the Muslims who stayed in Pale, many of them fought on the side of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you, sir, that this convoy was organised in an agreement with the other side, with the SDA party and its head for Pale, Ahmet Palo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmet would not have been capable as a human being or otherwise to organise something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is it still the position of counsel for Mr. Zupljanin that they decline to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. We don't have the cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Crncalo. Now, first of all, you were asked several questions earlier today about the existence or otherwise of detention centres in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up Exhibit P1465.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, what you will see in front of you is the map of Pale that you marked yesterday. And you'll see the building that you marked with number 2. You described that as being a cinema. And -- and you say that was the only building you know that operated as a prison or detention centre at that time. Now, Mr. Crncalo, was -- was that cinema building, do you know if it was ever used as a gym?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that there's another section in that building. I didn't go into every room there. But there is a part, a big part, that is cinema, where tickets were sold and snacks; and there was a door on the left where I never went through. And there was another door leading directly to the cinema hall where movies were shown. It's possible that there may have been other parts of that building that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know whether this building, the cinema building, was ever used as a cultural centre before the other building you've located as number 3 on the picture?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to Pale to attend high school in 1963. And, as a young man, I liked to go to the cinema. I know I went there to see movies. Now, as a community hall or something else, I think this used to be an old primary school that was used as a community hall, the one that I encircled as a sports hall. And then it was renovated, and social events took place there, and cultural events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry. If I may be of assistance. I don't think -- and I think it's important because 35, 16: I don't think that the witness mentioned a sport hall at all. What he was talking about was the -- the cultural hall. And also in line 15: Primary -- the old primary school that was used as a cultural hall, the one that I encircled as a cultural hall. And then it was renovated, and there was social, cultural events. Maybe you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: That is just what I was planning to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, when you talk about this building that you encircled, you said it used to be an old primary school that was used as a community hall. I just want to be clear, which building are you referring to? The building with which number on the map?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, which of these buildings that you've encircled was the one that used to be an old primary school and was then used as a cultural hall.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one with number 3 on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now to another point. You were asked some questions about the speech that Radovan Karadzic gave in Pale. And you were asked as to why you had never given the details of that speech before, or at least not until testifying in the Karadzic case. Now, when you testified in Krajisnik and you mentioned that Mr. Karadzic had given a speech in Pale, at that time, were you asked what the content of that speech was, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever asked me before about the contents of Karadzic's speech, when I mentioned he gave a speech at the cultural hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So until you were asked with -- asked by lawyers from the Office of the Prosecutor related to the Karadzic case, until that point, had you ever been asked for the exact content of that speech?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever asked me what Karadzic said at that rally, at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the final point I'd like to go over again with you is this issue of the house exchanges in relation to you moving out of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, could we please call up Exhibit P1464. And can we have page 2 of the English, please. Remaining on page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, do you see the entry for the exchange of your house at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And that's dated the 2nd of July, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The 2nd of July is the date that you were moved out of Pale on the convoy, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, in -- when you testified in Krajisnik, and you talked about the process of being moved out --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I'll just refer Your Honours and counsel to transcript page 5347 of that transcript, which is part of his proposed 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recall saying - sorry, I'll just find that - that instructions would be posted up and -- for the Muslim population, and they would be told which people from a particular area had to leave on a convoy on which particular day? Do you remember being told that? Oh, sorry, and do you remember testifying as to that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when I testified about that. There was an announcement on a sort of post, stuck to a lamppost, designating where the people should go to board the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you recall when you found out that you were going have to leave Pale? Was it the day that you had to leave; was it the day before? Are you able to remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that we had to leave the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So is it correct, then, that when Dragica Subotic came to your house and said she wanted to have your -- to exchange your property, at that point you already knew that you had to leave Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew I was leaving Pale the day before. And the day we were leaving, we went to the municipality to sign the contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And was it the day -- was that the -- the day that she first approached you to exchange your property?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: She didn't come before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just make a sort observation. I think we -- we are having a conflicting evidence in -- in the last -- in the last two or three questions which Mr. Dobbyn posed. And I would ask kindly if Mr. Dobbyn can explore more. Basically here is the -- what -- what I see as a problem: The witness testified that his late brother was in charge of negotiating the exchange of the -- of the property. Now, I think that Mr. Dobbyn has confused the witness with his answers because -- because the witness gave the answer that she came on the day when -- when they were exchanging the keys and she moved into -- into their property and they went into the bus, they boarded the bus. Obviously there has been a previous -- there must have been a previous contact between the -- his late brother and the -- and this lady that moved into their house. So maybe -- maybe this can be explored by Mr. Dobbyn. Because, like this, it would -- it wouldn't be very clear what is the evidence on -- on this issue by the witness. That is my observation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure if you share that observation, but, in my view, the evidence does seem clear: He found out -- he and presumably his brother found out the day before they had to leave Pale that they, in fact, had to leave. The day that they did have to leave, they were approached by this woman and told that she wanted to exchange houses with them. That's what I see on the record. What the -- what the witness has said, I'm -- I'm not sure what exactly needs to be clarified beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Dobbyn, it would be good to ask the witness, because I -- I'm somewhere in between the two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I'm sure you've heard what Their Honours have been saying and my learned counsel. Now, before the 2nd of July, the day that you moved out of Pale, do you know whether there was any contact between Dragica Subotic and your brother, with regards to exchanging the properties?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we found out that we had to leave, my brother had a big cow, and he said, What am I going to do with the cow? I said, You have to leave it. And he said, Do you think I could sell it to someone to get something for it, a bit of money? There was a crowd of people milling about, and he hadn't sold the cow. The day came when we had to leave. We were thinking, Where were we going go? Where were we going live? And, that day, a lot of people came to the street, which was called the 16 Muslim Brigade Street. There were two Serb houses at the beginning of the street, and Serb refugees probably knew we were leaving. So many people were suddenly there; you couldn't pass through. And as people were coming, they were trying to get to the houses first. And then this woman appeared, wanting to take our house in exchange, and he said, Shall I give it to her? I said, Swap it; do something. Then we went to the municipality, and we had to meet this deadline. We had to board the buses by 2.00. Everything had to be done by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, does that clarify the matter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, we thank you for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you. The usher will now escort you from the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, now that the witness has completed his testimony, I would move at this point to tender his 92 ter package which has 65 ter numbers 10390.01 to 10390.04.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me that that's had to be done, Mr. Dobbyn. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The -- the documents will become Exhibit 1466.1 through P1466.4, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready with its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, would you please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Good morning to you, sir. Would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Radomir Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, and what is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on 1st of January, 1950, and I'm an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any court in the -- in any of the countries in the former Yugoslavia in connection with these matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never testified before any court, international or national, in Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and the procedure that is followed here, in common with most courts, is that the side calling you would have the first opportunity to ask you questions and then the counsel representing the accused would have that opportunity as well. When counsel for the Prosecution who has called you have completed any re-examination that they have arising out of questions that the -- would have been asked by counsel of the accused, the Bench may have questions for you. You are scheduled to testify beginning today and into tomorrow, Wednesday, and the Prosecution has indicated that they would spend about two hours in examination-in-chief, and the -- counsel for the Defence will correct me if I have the arithmetic wrong, but I think the combined time that the Defence have asked for is two hours. The Court ordinarily sits - for your purposes this week, we are sitting morning - from 9.00 in the morning until 1.45 in the afternoon, because we have to make way for other trials which use this courtroom. But those sittings are not continuous, and indeed they do not extend for more than an hour and a half for technical reasons having to do with changing the tapes and whatnot. And, during that time, witnesses can take a -- have a comfort break. But, of course, if there is -- before the ordinary time that we would rise to take a break, if you need to take an adjourn -- if you need to have a break, you would indicate that to the Trial Chamber and we would, of course, accommodate you. So if you have understood those -- that explanation that I have given, I would now invite Mr. Di Fazio to begin his examination-in-chief of you. Sorry, one -- one other small matter. The -- you may have gathered that your testimony begins in the middle of a session, as it were, so actually we are scheduled to take the first break in your testimony within the next 11 minutes. And then we will have one more session before we rise for the day. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In addition to the matters relating to your personal background that the Trial Chamber asked you about, can you tell us if these details that I'm going to list to you are correct. You went to school and university in Sarajevo and graduated from the university in 1974 with a degree in mechanic engineering. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You started working at a place called the Famos factory, which is in Hrasnica, which is a suburb or area of Sarajevo city?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You started working there as a mechanical engineer, and you were promoted to chief of the development department there in 1990?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In fact, you continue working to this day as -- at the Famos factory, but in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There have been short breaks, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly. For a period of time, and could you give us the time, the period of time, you were the mayor of eastern Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was mayor of eastern Sarajevo from 2005 till 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You did your military service in the JNA at a place called Titov Veles in Macedonia, and that was in 1975 and 1976; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your testimony, I'm going to be asking you about a number of documents which are documents of or pertaining to the SDS. So the first question we need to sort out is this: Were you ever a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've never been officially a member of the SDS, but I was in a certain position to which the SDS delegated me, such as president of the Executive Committee in 1991 and 1992, as well as mayor of eastern Sarajevo in the time-period I've mentioned, 2005 till 2009, but without being a party member.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you ever on any SDS lists for the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At the first elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 24th of November, 1990, I was first on the list for the Ilidza municipality. I was on the list of the SDS for that municipality, Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now can you please explain briefly to the Trial Chamber how it was that you came to be on list of SDS members for Ilidza? What the circumstances were.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's not a list of the SDS members; it's a list compiled by the SDS party. How it came about? Well, actually it was a mere coincidence; namely, the then-representatives of the party, the SDS, in late 1990, were short of time. On the last day, they could submit their lists for the election in 1990; they didn't have enough members to register -- to put them on the list for Ilidza.
